current_episode.title: How to Break Into Commercial Real Estate With No Connections | Daynon Kirby

guest.bio_context: Daymond Kirby was born on an Army post in Panama, moved to Ann Arbor, Michigan where his father earned an MBA from University of Michigan, then relocated to Phoenix where he played college soccer. He started his commercial real estate career in June 2020 and obtained his CCIM designation in 2023. He previously worked for Family Video before founding the Black Foundation, a 501c3 private foundation focused on providing career pathways to minorities and veterans in commercial real estate.

pending_qa.q: How should someone with no connections break into commercial real estate as a career in their 20s?
pending_qa.r: The first step is education and understanding the different pathways available—broker, investor, developer, property manager, asset manager, or other roles. Most people get into commercial real estate through relationships, but if you don't have those, joining a collaborative team is more sustainable than starting alone. You should seek a team doing many transactions so you get educational reps; even if you're low on the totem pole, you gain knowledge and sustainable cash flow while learning. If you join a boutique firm, you may need to create an official team arrangement or bring something of immediate value—like social media marketing or AI skills—rather than being purely a time drain while being trained.

pending_qa.q: What are the two distinct economic models for career paths, and how do they apply to commercial real estate roles?
pending_qa.r: There is the time and effort economy where people are paid for showing up and doing the work, and the results economy where income depends on producing results regardless of hours worked. Traditionally, commercial real estate has been results-focused, but the industry is shifting to include more time-and-effort roles like property managers and salary-based positions with base pay and commission blends. Not everyone is suited for results-based compensation; some people value security and a stable paycheck, while others need the freedom to control their income and not be held back, and understanding which economy you belong in is crucial for career satisfaction.

pending_qa.q: What educational pathways does the Black Foundation offer across different career stages?
pending_qa.r: Education offerings depend on career cycle: middle and high school students receive career day representation, mindset manifestation, and thinking bigger exercises; juniors and seniors learn how to obtain a real estate license at age 18 and receive support; college students participate in panels, Q&A sessions, and workshops; and adults already in or interested in commercial real estate can access guidance, CCIM preparation, career placement help, and resources to be successful from beginning to end of their journey.

pending_qa.q: How does accessing knowledge and opportunity in commercial real estate create wealth and break cycles of poverty?
pending_qa.r: Daymond Kirby explains that the Black Foundation brings together parties that have traditionally been disconnected by design—talented, motivated, and driven people who simply need access to knowledge and opportunity. The foundation operates as a 'hand up, not a handout,' focusing on people already showing they are willing to put in the work, and gives them all resources needed to succeed. By democratizing access to commercial real estate knowledge and connections, individuals can become brokers, investors, or developers, control their paychecks, build wealth, and ultimately leave a family legacy.

pending_qa.q: What specific value can younger professionals bring to established commercial real estate teams to justify immediate hiring?
pending_qa.r: Young professionals should walk into a team with something of immediate value rather than being a pure time drain while being trained. Examples include offering social media marketing, video production skills, or—particularly relevant now—proficiency with AI tools. Daymond Kirby notes that the younger generation's ease with AI is an incredible asset that commercial real estate, which has traditionally lagged in technology adoption, is desperately seeking, and this can be leveraged as a differentiator when joining an established firm.
